4.2.1.examLens: Recognize when a straight line is the wrong model and choose between a linear and a curved fit.

worked.question: A linear fit gives R² = 0.82 and a U-shaped residual plot. Adding an X² term raises R² to 0.96, the X² term has p = 0.001, and the residuals now look random. What do you choose?
worked.solution: The quadratic model. The U-shaped residuals showed the linear form was wrong, the new term is significant, and the residuals are now random. The higher R² is supported by the diagnostics, not just by the extra term.

4.2.2.examLens: Interpret an output table, spot multicollinearity, and decide which terms to keep.

worked.question: A model for cycle time has predictors Temperature (p = 0.03), Pressure (p = 0.41), Speed (p = 0.002), and Operator experience (p = 0.38). Overall F is significant, R² = 0.88, and the VIFs for Temperature and Pressure are 14 and 12. (a) What is going on with Temperature and Pressure? (b) What should you do?
worked.solution:
(a) VIFs of 14 and 12 are well above 5, so Temperature and Pressure are strongly collinear: they carry overlapping information. That can inflate the standard errors and make individual p-values unreliable.
(b) Refit removing one at a time, highest p-value first (Pressure at 0.41, then Operator experience at 0.38 if it still has a high p-value), checking VIFs and adjusted R² at each step. Keep the model simple and see whether the Temperature coefficient stabilizes.

4.2.3.examLens: Decide which interval answers the question asked. The wording tells you.

worked.question: At X = 10, software gives a 95% CI of (48.1, 51.9) and a 95% PI of (42.0, 58.0). (a) Which answers "what will the next part measure?" (b) Which answers "what is the long-run average at X = 10?" (c) Why is one wider?
worked.solution: (a) The prediction interval (42.0 to 58.0). (b) The confidence interval (48.1 to 51.9). (c) The prediction interval also has to cover the scatter of individual parts around the average, not just the uncertainty about where the average is.

4.2.4.examLens: Interpret the standard residual plots together and name what is wrong.

worked.question: A four-in-one plot shows: the probability plot is close to a straight line; residuals versus fits show a clear funnel; residuals versus order look random. What is wrong and what is a reasonable fix?
worked.solution: The errors look normal and independent, but the variance is not constant (funnel). A reasonable fix is to transform Y (for example with a Box-Cox transformation, see 4.2.5) and refit.

4.2.5.examLens: Read a Box-Cox plot, pick a transformation, and know when not to bother.

worked.question: Box-Cox output for a response with strictly positive values shows an optimal λ = 0.08 with a 95% confidence interval of −0.30 to 0.45. Another response shows an optimal λ = 0.60 with an interval of 0.20 to 1.20. What do you do in each case?
worked.solution:
First response: the interval (−0.30 to 0.45) does not contain 1 but does contain 0, so a transformation is appropriate. Choose a rounded, interpretable value inside the interval: λ = 0 (natural log). The square root (0.5) falls just outside the interval.
Second response: the interval contains 1, so no transformation may be needed even though the optimal λ is 0.60.

4.2.1.a.title: Fitting curves
4.2.1.a.html: When the relationship bends, fit a quadratic (Y = b0 + b1X + b2X²) or cubic term, or transform X or Y (for example take the log) so the relationship becomes straight.

4.2.1.b.title: The curved-residual clue
4.2.1.b.html: A curved pattern in the residuals (residuals versus fits) tells you a straight line is not enough and a non-linear fit is needed.

4.2.1.c.title: Higher R² is not always better
4.2.1.c.html: Adding terms always raises R², even when they only fit noise. A complicated curve can match the data very closely and then predict new data badly (overfitting). Prefer the simplest model that fits well, and check adjusted R² and residuals.

4.2.1.d.title: Linear or quadratic?
4.2.1.d.html: From a fitted-line plot, choose the quadratic when the data clearly curve, the residuals of the linear fit show a pattern, and the quadratic term is significant. Choose the linear model when the quadratic adds almost nothing.

4.2.2.a.title: The model
4.2.2.a.html: Ŷ = b0 + b1X1 + b2X2 + ... + bkXk. Each coefficient is the change in Y for a one-unit change in that X with the other X's held constant.

4.2.2.b.title: The tests
4.2.2.b.html:
• Overall F-test: is at least one predictor useful? (H0: all slopes are zero.)
  • Individual t-tests: is this predictor useful given the others in the model?
  • Adjusted R²: like R² but penalizes useless terms, so it can fall when a term does not help.

4.2.2.c.title: Multicollinearity
4.2.2.c.html:
Predictors that are strongly correlated with each other. The VIF (variance inflation factor) measures it: VIF = 1 ÷ (1 − R²j), where R²j comes from regressing predictor j on the other predictors. A VIF above 5 (some use 10) is a rule-of-thumb warning, not a fixed cutoff.
Symptom: a high overall F and R², but individually insignificant t-tests. The model fits well, but the data cannot tell which of the overlapping predictors matters.

4.2.2.d.title: Building the model
4.2.2.d.html: Common approaches: stepwise and best subsets. Keep the model parsimonious: as simple as possible while still explaining the data well.

4.2.2.e.title: Interaction terms
4.2.2.e.html: An interaction (X1 × X2) means the effect of one predictor depends on the level of another. Example: a temperature change matters more at high pressure than at low pressure.

4.2.2.f.title: Categorical predictors
4.2.2.f.html: Shift, supplier, and machine enter the model as indicator (dummy) variables. Recognition only: you will not need to code them by hand.

4.2.2.g.title: Removing terms
4.2.2.g.html: Backward elimination is standard: drop the term with the highest p-value, refit, and repeat. Two cautions: keep the lower-order terms of any interaction you retain, and do not drop a term on p-value alone when it matters for the purpose of the model. Adjusted R² can fall when a term is useless.

4.2.2.h.title: Interaction hierarchy
4.2.2.h.html: If an interaction stays in the model, keep its main effects even if a main effect's p-value is weak.

4.2.2.i.title: Mallows' Cp
4.2.2.i.html: Extension, glossary only. A model-selection statistic. Low exam yield.

4.2.3.a.title: Confidence interval for the mean response
4.2.3.a.html: A range for the average Y at a given X. It reflects uncertainty in the line itself.

4.2.3.b.title: Prediction interval for a single observation
4.2.3.b.html: A range for one future individual value at a given X. It includes the uncertainty in the line plus the natural scatter of individual values, so it is always wider than the confidence interval at the same X.

4.2.3.c.title: Shape
4.2.3.c.html: Both intervals are narrowest at the mean of X and widen as X moves away from it. That is another reason not to extrapolate.

4.2.3.d.title: Which interval for one new unit?

4.2.3.e.title: Wording cue
4.2.3.e.html: "What is the average output at X = 10?" means a confidence interval. "What will the next unit be at X = 10?" means a prediction interval.

4.2.4.a.title: The same four residual checks
4.2.4.a.html: The residual checks from SG-4.1.3 apply: normal probability plot, residuals versus fits, residuals versus order, and a histogram of residuals. Together they are often shown as the four-in-one residual plot.

4.2.4.b.title: Added checks for multiple regression
4.2.4.b.html: Also look at VIF (multicollinearity), leverage (unusual combinations of X values), and influence (points that change the fit a lot).

4.2.4.c.title: Cook's distance
4.2.4.c.html: Extension. Cook's distance is one statistic that measures how much a single point influences the fit. Recognize "influential observation"; the formula is not needed.

4.2.4.d.title: Interpret the four-pack
4.2.4.d.html: Combine the plots into one diagnosis. Points off the line on the probability plot suggest non-normal errors. A funnel on residuals versus fits suggests unequal variance. A pattern versus order suggests dependence or a time effect. One extreme point on every plot suggests a possible influential outlier.

4.2.5.a.title: Why transform
4.2.5.a.html: A transformation reshapes the data so that normality or constant variance holds better, which makes analysis and regression more reliable.

4.2.5.b.title: The Box-Cox lambda
4.2.5.b.html:
Box-Cox raises the data to a power λ (lambda).

  • λ = 1: no transformation.
  • λ = 0.5: square root.
  • λ = 0: natural log (by definition, as a limit).
  • λ = −1: reciprocal.

The software finds the best λ.

4.2.5.c.title: Positive data only
4.2.5.c.html: Box-Cox needs positive data. For zeros or negatives, add a constant to every value first.

4.2.5.d.title: Johnson transformation
4.2.5.d.html: Extension, glossary only. A more flexible transformation that can handle a wider range of data. Low exam yield.

4.2.5.e.title: Transform the spec limits too
4.2.5.e.html: If you transform the data and then do a capability analysis, transform the specification limits the same way.

4.2.5.f.title: Reading the output
4.2.5.f.html: The plot shows the best (optimal) λ and a confidence interval for λ. Choose a transformation from that.

4.2.5.g.title: The λ interval rule
4.2.5.g.html: If the confidence interval for λ contains 1, no transformation may be needed, even if the optimal λ is not exactly 1. Otherwise, pick a rounded, interpretable λ inside the interval (for example 0.5 for square root, or 0 for log).

4.2.1-1.stem: A linear fit gives R² = 0.82 and a U-shaped residual plot. Adding an X² term raises R² to 0.96, the X² term has p = 0.001, and the residuals now look random. Which model should be chosen?

options.html: The linear model, because it is simpler
The quadratic model, because the diagnostics support the curved form
A model with as many terms as possible

4.2.1-1.explanation: The U-shaped residuals showed the straight line was wrong, the new term is significant, and the new residuals are random.

4.2.1-2.stem: Adding a term to a regression model can never lower R², so a higher R² alone does not prove the added term is useful.
4.2.1-2.explanation: R² never decreases when a term is added, even if the term only fits noise. Adjusted R², residuals, and parsimony help guard against overfitting.

4.2.2-1.stem: For one predictor, regressing it on the other predictors gives R² = 0.90. What is its VIF?
4.2.2-1.explanation: VIF = 1 ÷ (1 − R²) = 1 ÷ 0.10 = 10, well above the rule-of-thumb warning level of 5.

4.2.2-2.stem: A model has a high overall F and a high R², but none of the individual predictor t-tests is significant. What is the most likely cause?
4.2.2-2.explanation: The model fits well overall, but overlapping predictors share their information, so individual tests cannot tell them apart.

4.2.2-3.stem: Using backward elimination, a team removes terms one at a time. Which term should be considered for removal first?

options.html: The term with the lowest p-value
The term with the highest p-value
The term with the largest coefficient

4.2.2-3.explanation: Drop the term with the highest p-value, refit, and repeat, while keeping lower-order terms of any interaction that stays.

4.2.2-4.stem: A model contains the interaction A × B. The main effect of A has a weak p-value, but the interaction is significant. What should the team do?

options.html: Remove A, because its p-value is weak
Keep A, because the model keeps the main effects of any interaction that remains

4.2.2-4.explanation: Keep the main effects when the interaction stays, even when a main effect's own p-value is weak.

4.2.2-5.stem: Adjusted R² can decrease when a useless predictor is added to the model.
4.2.2-5.explanation: Adjusted R² penalizes terms that do not help, so it can fall when a term adds nothing.

4.2.2-6.stem: A model needs to include which of three suppliers a part came from. How does a categorical predictor like this enter the regression?
4.2.2-6.explanation: Categorical predictors such as shift, supplier, or machine enter the model as indicator variables.

4.2.3-1.stem: At X = 10 the software gives a 95% confidence interval of 48.1 to 51.9 and a 95% prediction interval of 42.0 to 58.0. A manager asks, "What will the next unit measure at X = 10?" Which interval answers it?

options.html: The confidence interval, because it is narrower
The prediction interval, because it covers a single future unit

4.2.3-1.explanation: A single future value needs the prediction interval, which includes individual scatter as well as uncertainty in the mean.

4.2.3-2.stem: At the same X, a prediction interval is narrower than the confidence interval.
4.2.3-2.explanation: The prediction interval is always wider because it includes the scatter of individual units.

4.2.3-3.stem: Where are confidence and prediction intervals narrowest?

options.html: At the mean of X, widening as X moves away
They are the same width everywhere

4.2.3-3.explanation: Both intervals widen as X moves away from the center of the data.

4.2.4-1.stem: A four-in-one residual plot shows a probability plot close to a straight line, a clear funnel on residuals versus fits, and a random pattern versus order. What is wrong, and what is a reasonable fix?

options.html: The errors are not normal; remove outliers
The variance is not constant; transform the response and refit
The observations are dependent; collect data in order

4.2.4-1.explanation: A funnel shows non-constant variance. A transformation (for example Box-Cox) is a common fix.

4.2.4-2.stem: Which additional checks are added for multiple regression compared with simple regression?

options.html: A control chart for each predictor

4.2.4-2.explanation: Multiple regression adds multicollinearity (VIF) and leverage and influence checks to the standard residual checks.

4.2.5-1.stem: A Box-Cox analysis suggests λ = 0.5. Which transformation is that?
4.2.5-1.explanation: λ = 1 is no transform, 0.5 is square root, 0 is natural log, and −1 is reciprocal.

4.2.5-2.stem: A Box-Cox plot shows an optimal λ of 0.60 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.20 to 1.20. What is the best conclusion?

options.html: No transformation may be needed, because the interval contains 1

4.2.5-2.explanation: If the confidence interval for λ contains 1, no transformation may be needed even if the optimal λ is not exactly 1.

4.2.5-3.stem: A response has some values equal to zero. What must be done before applying a Box-Cox transformation?

options.html: Add a constant to every value so all are positive

4.2.5-3.explanation: Box-Cox requires strictly positive data, so shift the values by a constant first.

4.2.2-1.text: Regressing one predictor on the other predictors gives R² = 0.3. What is its VIF, and is it a concern?
4.2.2-1.answer: VIF = 1 ÷ (1 − 0.3) = 1.43. It is below 5, so it is not a concern by the usual rule of thumb.

4.2.2-2.text: Regressing one predictor on the other predictors gives R² = 0.5. What is its VIF, and is it a concern?
4.2.2-2.answer: VIF = 1 ÷ (1 − 0.5) = 2.00. It is below 5, so it is not a concern by the usual rule of thumb.

4.2.2-3.text: Regressing one predictor on the other predictors gives R² = 0.75. What is its VIF, and is it a concern?
4.2.2-3.answer: VIF = 1 ÷ (1 − 0.75) = 4.00. It is below 5, so it is not a concern by the usual rule of thumb.

4.2.2-4.text: Regressing one predictor on the other predictors gives R² = 0.8. What is its VIF, and is it a concern?
4.2.2-4.answer: VIF = 1 ÷ (1 − 0.8) = 5.00. It is above the rule-of-thumb warning level of 5, so multicollinearity is a concern.

4.2.2-5.text: Regressing one predictor on the other predictors gives R² = 0.9. What is its VIF, and is it a concern?
4.2.2-5.answer: VIF = 1 ÷ (1 − 0.9) = 10.00. It is above the rule-of-thumb warning level of 5, so multicollinearity is a concern.

4.2.2-6.text: Regressing one predictor on the other predictors gives R² = 0.95. What is its VIF, and is it a concern?
4.2.2-6.answer: VIF = 1 ÷ (1 − 0.95) = 20.00. It is above the rule-of-thumb warning level of 5, so multicollinearity is a concern.

4.2.2-7.text: A model with n = 20 observations and k = 2 predictors has R² = 0.8. What is the adjusted R²?

4.2.2-8.text: A model with n = 25 observations and k = 3 predictors has R² = 0.7. What is the adjusted R²?

4.2.2-9.text: A model with n = 20 observations and k = 2 predictors has R² = 0.9. What is the adjusted R²?

4.2.2-10.text: A model with n = 20 observations and k = 2 predictors has R² = 0.6. What is the adjusted R²?

4.2.5-1.text: A Box-Cox analysis suggests λ = 0.5. Which transformation is that, and what are the transformed values of 16, 16, 1, 16?
4.2.5-1.answer: λ = 0.5 is the square root. Transformed values: 4.000, 4.000, 1.000, 4.000.

4.2.5-2.text: A Box-Cox analysis suggests λ = 0. Which transformation is that, and what are the transformed values of 5, 16, 10, 25?
4.2.5-2.answer: λ = 0 is the natural log. Transformed values: 1.609, 2.773, 2.303, 3.219.

4.2.5-3.text: A Box-Cox analysis suggests λ = -1. Which transformation is that, and what are the transformed values of 1, 9, 5, 2?

4.2.5-4.text: A Box-Cox analysis suggests λ = 1. Which transformation is that, and what are the transformed values of 25, 9, 16, 2?
4.2.5-4.answer: λ = 1 is the no transformation. Transformed values: 25.000, 9.000, 16.000, 2.000.
